newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico ruling party patriarch denies drug links.
newsitem.headline: Mexico ruling party patriarch denies drug links.

text.p: The father of former Mexican President Carlos Salinas de Gortari denied on Wednesday any link to drug trafficking and said a New York Times article alleging he was involved in the drugs trade was false.

"I sustain categorically that neither my family nor I has ever had any link to any drug trafficker," Raul Salinas Lozano, a patriarch of the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), said in a statement.

The New York Times said in an article published on Wednesday that his longtime private secretary in statements to U.S. authorities had implicated Salinas Lozano, one of his other sons Raul Salinas de Gortari and his former son-in-law Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu in narcotics dealings.

The newspaper said the woman, named as Magdalena Ruiz Pelayo, was cooperating with federal prosecutors in Houston who are seeking to confiscate $9 million from Mario Ruiz Massieu, brother of Jose Francisco, on grounds that the money is drug-tainted.
Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu was assassinated in September 1994 and Raul Salinas de Gortari is in jail on charges of having masterminded the killing.
Raul Salinas Lozano, a former Mexican senator and cabinet member in the 1960s, denied in his statement that Ruiz Pelayo had been his private secretary, as The New York Times said.
"I roundly deny that statement and demand that the lady in question prove it with solid facts," he said.

"It is an aberration that such a serious newspaper should not have verified the statements of this lady, who was in prison in Mexico from 1989 and in the United States in 1992, without ever mentioning me or my family."
He said Ruiz Pelayo also went by the name of Magdalena Pineda Trinidad and that her statements were "a big lie."

The New York Times said Ruiz Pelayo was convicted of drug trafficking at a trial in Newark, N.J. in 1992 and that court documents from the case showed she had worked as private secretary to Salinas Lozano.
The New York Times article was the latest twist in a series of interlocking scandals in Mexico involving drug trafficking, political murder and allegations of corruption in high places.

It also coincided with a heated debate in Washington and Mexico City about whether President Bill Clinton should "certify" by the end of this month that Mexico is cooperating with the United States in its war on illegal drugs.
